BioNova Therapeutics - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the BioNova Therapeutics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. As a reminder, please do not use your telephone keypad during the presentation portion of the call. To ask a question during the Q&A, press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star then two. Today's conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss BioNova Therapeutics' financial results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Dr. Lisa Ramirez, Chief Medical Officer; Dr. Raj Patel, Chief Scientific Officer; Dr. Elena Vasquez, Head of Commercial; and Tom Rivera, Head of Manufacturing.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's call will contain forward-looking statements. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Johnathan Hale, CEO of BioNova Therapeutics.

Johnathan Hale, CEO:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. BioNova Therapeutics delivered a strong performance in the third quarter, driven by robust commercial execution on our blockbuster franchises, key pipeline milestones, and disciplined cost management. We continue to make significant progress on our key strategic priorities, including advancing our clinical programs through phase progressions and data readouts, securing regulatory approvals and label expansions, executing transformative business development deals, growing product revenues across our key franchises, enhancing marketing and sales effectiveness, expanding gross margins through manufacturing efficiencies, and proactively addressing patent cliff exposures with comprehensive life cycle management strategies.

We are particularly excited about Zepara and its potential to transform outcomes in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and beyond through upcoming label expansions.

Now, I will turn the call over to Michael Chen, our CFO, to provide a more detailed review of our financial results.

Michael Chen, CFO:
Thank you, Johnathan. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a solid third quarter. Revenue for the quarter was $2.85 billion, an increase of 18% compared to the same period last year. This increase was primarily driven by volume growth in our oncology and immunology franchises, along with the ramp of our emerging GLP-1 product.

Our GAAP net income for the quarter was $620 million, or $2.45 per share. Non-GAAP net income was $780 million, or $3.10 per share.

Our operating expenses were $1.2 billion, reflecting continued investment in R&D to support our pipeline while optimizing our cost structure. We continue to invest in R&D to support our pipeline. Our cash position remains strong at $2.8 billion.

For the full year, we are updating our guidance to revenue of $11.0 to $11.3 billion.

Good afternoon, everyone. As we dive into our financial results, I'd like to focus on our product revenue performance, which totaled $2.85 billion for the quarter, up 18% year-over-year and 7% sequentially from Q2. This growth was driven primarily by our core franchises in oncology and immunology, partially offset by expected biosimilar pressures in our legacy rare disease portfolio. Excluding foreign exchange impacts, which headwinded us by 2 points due to a stronger USD, underlying growth was 20%.

Let me break this down by our four key drug franchises—Oncology, Immunology, Rare Diseases, and Emerging Therapies—providing granular volume and price analysis. We'll reference average selling price, or ASP, net of discounts, rebates, and chargebacks; volume in terms of standardized patient-days on therapy, or PDOTs, which aligns with our defined daily dose metrics; and total prescriptions, or TRx, sourced from IQVIA data. All figures are in USD.

Oncology Franchise: $1.42 billion, +24% YoY, +9% Q/Q (52% of total product revenue).

Our oncology portfolio, led by our PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor NovaKine-7 and the recently launched bispecific antibody NovaTarg-X for solid tumors, continues to outperform. Franchise revenue reached $1.42 billion, capturing 28% U.S. market share in non-small cell lung cancer checkpoint inhibitors, up from 22% a year ago, per Symphony Health.

Volume: 2.8 million PDOTs, +19% YoY. NovaKine-7 drove the bulk at 2.1 million PDOTs (+22% YoY), fueled by a 15% increase in new patient starts, or NRx, to 145,000—benefiting from our label expansion into frontline triple-negative breast cancer approved by the FDA in Q1. NovaTarg-X contributed 450,000 PDOTs in its first full quarter post-launch, with TRx growth of 35% sequentially as we ramped U.S. and EU5 field force expansion. Share gains versus Merck's Keytruda and Bristol Myers' Opdivo were evident in NSCLC, where we gained 4 points of market share through our real-world evidence from the Phase IV NovaReal study.

Price: ASP held steady at $168,000 per patient-year for NovaKine-7, flat YoY despite 42% gross-to-net adjustments from PBM rebates under the Inflation Reduction Act. NovaTarg-X launched at a WAC of $22,500 per dose, with realized ASP of $19,800 after initial contracting—premium pricing justified by its 25% ORR improvement in HER2-low breast cancer per our pivotal trial.

Regionally, U.S. was 72% of franchise sales ($1.02 billion, +27% YoY), EU 18% ($256 million, +15% YoY post-EMA approval), and RoW 10% ($142 million, +22% YoY) with strong traction in China via our partnership with Sinopharm. Headwinds included 3% volume erosion from Keytruda biosimilars entering Japan.

Immunology Franchise: $892 million, +14% YoY, +5% Q/Q (31% of total).

ImmunoBlock RA, our IL-6/IL-23 dual inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis, and the follow-on subcutaneous formulation ImmunoBlock SC, powered $892 million in revenue—maintaining #2 position behind AbbVie's Humira in the U.S. RA market at 19% share.

Volume: 4.2 million PDOTs, +12% YoY. ImmunoBlock RA saw 3.1 million PDOTs (+10% YoY) with stable TRx of 620,000 amid biosimilar competition from Samsung Bioepis' Hadlima equivalent. ImmunoBlock SC ramped to 1.1 million PDOTs (+45% YoY), capturing 12% of the RA switcher market as patients migrate from IV therapies—our PROMPT trial data showed 30% better adherence rates.

Price: Blended ASP of $42,500 per patient-year, +2% YoY. We implemented targeted price increases in non-contracted channels, offset by 38% gross-to-net from 340B and Medicaid clawbacks. ImmunoBlock SC priced at a 15% premium to RA ($48,000 ASP) to reflect its convenience.

U.S. dominated at 68% ($607 million, +16% YoY), EU 22% ($196 million, flat YoY due to HTA delays in Germany), and RoW 10% ($89 million, +12% YoY) via tenders in Brazil. Strategic initiative: Our co-formulation with methotrexate in Phase III, aiming for 2025 approval to counter JAK inhibitor erosion.

Rare Diseases Franchise: $356 million, -8% YoY, flat Q/Q (12% of total).

GeneFix-HemA, our AAV8 gene therapy for hemophilia A, and enzyme replacement therapy NovaZyme for Fabry disease generated $356 million. Performance reflects full-year biosimilar headwinds post-patent expiry on legacy products.

Volume: 1.1 million PDOTs, -5% YoY. GeneFix-HemA held at 850,000 PDOTs (-2% YoY) with 2,400 one-time treatments, buoyed by bleed reduction data from our long-term registry (annualized bleed rate down 92% vs. standard prophylaxis). NovaZyme volumes declined 18% to 250,000 PDOTs due to Roche's Fabrazyme generics.

Price: ASP down 3% YoY to $2.1 million per GeneFix treatment (net of outcomes-based rebates, now at 25% of contracts). NovaZyme ASP at $450,000 per patient-year, -10% from pricing reforms.

U.S. 60% ($214 million, -6% YoY), EU 25% ($89 million, -12% YoY from NICE restrictions), RoW 15% ($53 million, flat). Initiative: Scale-up of our Shelbyville, NC facility added 50% capacity for GeneFix, targeting 3,000 treatments annually by 2026.

Emerging Therapies Franchise: $182 million, +62% YoY, +22% Q/Q (6% of total).

Our GLP-1/GIP dual agonist SlimVira for obesity and T2D launched in June, hitting $182 million—faster than Novo Nordisk's Wegovy ramp.

Volume: 650,000 PDOTs, +62% from launch baseline. NRx hit 180,000 in the U.S., with 14% market share in branded GLP-1s per IQVIA.

Price: ASP $14,200 per patient-year, flat from launch WAC of $15,000 after early PBM pushback.

U.S. 92% ($167 million), early EU pilots. Upside from our oral formulation in Phase III.

Across franchises, volume drove 65% of growth, price 20%, and FX/mix 15%. Key initiatives include AI-optimized manufacturing yielding 15% COGS reduction, and our $1.2 billion M&A war chest post-Vertex-like deal for a CRISPR editing platform. We expect Q4 franchise growth of 16-20%, full-year product revenue at $11.0-11.3 billion. Pricing pressures from the IRA cap will intensify in 2026, but label expansions and combos position us for 12-15% CAGR through 2028.

As we dive further into our financial results, I'd like to spend some time on gross margin trends and the manufacturing efficiencies driving them, as these are core to our long-term value creation in the competitive biotech landscape.

Starting with the headline: our consolidated gross margin expanded to 84.2% in Q3, up 320 basis points year-over-year from 81.0% and 110 basis points sequentially from Q2's 83.1%. This marks our sixth straight quarter of gross margin expansion, putting us on track for a full-year outlook of 83-85%. For context, this outperforms the pharma industry average of around 78-80%, as reported in recent IQVIA data, and positions us favorably against peers like Regeneron, which posted 83% last quarter, or Amgen at 79%.

Let me break this down by key drivers. First, product mix and volume leverage. Our flagship asset, XYZumab—a PD-1 inhibitor akin to Keytruda—drove 62% of revenue and delivered a segment gross margin of 88.5%, up from 86.2% YoY. This was fueled by a 22% volume increase from U.S. and EU demand, outpacing the 15% blended pricing erosion we guided to due to payer pushback. Importantly, COGS per 100mg vial fell 12% to $1,450, thanks to scale at our full-capacity Holly Springs, NC facility. Conversely, our legacy small-molecule portfolio, like hypertension med ZYBlock, saw margins dip to 72% from pricing pressures in emerging markets, but this was more than offset by the high-margin biologics shift, now 78% of our mix versus 65% last year.

Manufacturing efficiency is the real story here, accounting for roughly 60% of the margin expansion. We've realized $145 million in COGS savings YTD, beating our $120 million target, primarily through yield improvements and process optimizations across our network.

On the biologics side, our monoclonal antibody platform saw average bioreactor yields climb 18% YoY to 5.2 g/L in perfusion mode, rivaling what we've seen from Lonza partnerships. This stems from our Q4 2023 rollout of continuous manufacturing at our Singapore site—our first Asia hub, operational since H2 2023. Using GE Healthcare's ReadyToProcess WAVE systems with single-use bioreactors, we've cut changeover times by 40% and reduced media costs by 25%. For XYZumab specifically, upstream productivity hit 6.1 g/L, enabling us to defer $300 million in capex for a new U.S. train.

Downstream, we're leveraging AI-driven process analytical technology (PAT), integrated with our Rockwell Automation DCS systems. Predictive analytics have slashed chromatography resin fouling by 30%, dropping purification costs from $450 to $320 per gram of purified protein. This mirrors efficiencies at Samsung Biologics, where similar tech yielded 15-20% COGS reductions.

Regionally, margins vary but are trending up everywhere: U.S. (55% of production): 86% margins, bolstered by TCJA tax credits and our Rhode Island fill-finish site's automation, which hit 99.5% right-first-time yields. Europe (25%, primarily Ireland): 82% margins, resilient despite EMA serialization mandates; we've offset 4% raw material inflation via local API sourcing, avoiding the 10% Eurozone API shortages peers like Novartis faced. Asia-Pacific (20%, Singapore/China JVs): 79% margins but fastest growth at 28% YoY, with lower labor and energy costs—electricity at $0.08/kWh versus $0.15 in the U.S.—driving strategic insourcing of biosimilars ahead of Humira patent cliffs.

We've also navigated headwinds adeptly. Raw material inflation eased to 3% QoQ from 7% peaks, thanks to multi-year contracts with AGC Biologics for cell culture media. Supply chain resilience post-COVID—echoing lessons from the 2022 heparin crisis—includes dual-sourcing 90% of critical excipients and $50 million in strategic inventory.

Looking forward, our strategic initiatives will sustain this trajectory: Next-gen capacity: $450 million investment in a continuous flow chemistry plant for ADCs, targeting 90%+ margins by FY2026, inspired by Seagen's tech pre-Pfizer acquisition. Biosimilar ramp: Launching three by YE2024, with modeled COGS at 35-40% of originators, leveraging our high-yield CHO-K1 cell lines. Sustainability push: PATCO2 capture in fermentation cuts energy use 15%, aligning with EU CBAM tariffs and unlocking grants. Digital twin modeling: Partnering with AspenTech for virtual plant simulations, projecting another 10% yield uplift by mid-2025.

In summary, our gross margins are not just expanding—they're structurally improving through tech-led efficiencies, positioning BioNova to capture share in a $1.5 trillion market growing at 8% CAGR per Evaluate Pharma. We remain committed to 85%+ long-term margins as we scale.

Thank you, Johnathan, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our business development activities, which continue to be a cornerstone of our strategy to build a robust, diversified pipeline across high-growth modalities in oncology, immunology, and gene therapy. In Q3, we executed three transformative transactions—a milestone licensing deal, a strategic tuck-in acquisition, and a co-development partnership—that not only de-risk our portfolio but also position us to capture significant value in a market where global BD activity reached $150 billion year-to-date, up 25% from last year, driven by big pharma's scramble for next-gen assets amid patent cliffs on blockbusters like Keytruda and Stelara.

Let me start with licensing. Earlier this month, we announced an exclusive global licensing agreement with Ascend Biotech, a Cambridge-based stealth-mode company, for their lead asset, ASC-301, a next-generation T-cell engager targeting CD19/CD3 for relapsed/refractory B-cell lymphomas. This bispecific antibody leverages a novel tumor-microenvironment modulating domain that enhances NK cell infiltration, showing a 65% ORR and 40% CR rate in heavily pretreated patients from their Phase 1b data readout last quarter—benchmarks that rival the best-in-class data from Genentech's Columvi. We're paying $175 million upfront, with potential milestones totaling $1.2 billion across regulatory, clinical, and commercial hurdles, plus tiered royalties starting at 18% on net sales, escalating to 24% above $1 billion annually. This deal fits seamlessly into our hematologic malignancies franchise, where we see a $15 billion TAM by 2030, and it accelerates our entry into the solid tumor space via planned Phase 2 expansion into HER2-low breast cancer.

Complementing this, we out-licensed ex-U.S. and ex-EU rights to our proprietary ADC, NOV-ADC-456—a folate receptor alpha-targeted payload conjugate with a cleavable topoisomerase inhibitor linker—to Sinopharm's innovation arm in China. This transaction reflects the growing trend of regional carve-outs, with China representing 20% of global BD volume this year per Evaluate Pharma data. We received $120 million upfront, $800 million in biobucks tied to China NDA approval and peak sales milestones, and double-digit royalties in the mid-teens. Strategically, this mitigates our China market risk while unlocking non-dilutive capital to fund NOV-ADC-456's ongoing pivotal trial in ovarian cancer, where interim data showed a 52% confirmed response rate at the RP2D—outperforming standard care PFS by 8 months. Regionally, this deal underscores our focus on Greater China partnerships, where patient access to late-line therapies is exploding due to reimbursement reforms under the NRDL, and it positions Sinopharm to leverage their 300 million+ covered lives for rapid market penetration.

Shifting to acquisitions, we closed our $650 million acquisition of Helix Genomics, a San Diego-based CRISPR/Cas13 platform company specializing in RNA-targeted gene editing for neuromuscular diseases. Helix brings two clinical-stage assets: HLX-102, a Cas13a nuclease editing DMD mutations with 75% exon-skipping efficiency in NHP models, entering Phase 1/2 next year; and HLX-205, targeting ALS via STMN2 upregulation, with preclinical durability exceeding 12 months post-single dose. This bolt-on deal, structured with 60% cash and 40% stock at a 4.2x multiple to Helix's 2023 revenue run-rate, adds $300 million in anticipated R&D tax credits from California's AB 135 program and bolsters our rare disease footprint, where orphan drug designations yield pricing power averaging 5x higher than non-orphans.

The acquisition expands our gene therapy capabilities beyond AAV vectors into programmable RNA editors, aligning with industry shifts—note Sarepta's $7.7 billion Roche deal and Beam Therapeutics' $300 million upfront from Eli Lilly for base editing. Post-close synergies include integrating Helix's proprietary LNP delivery tech with our lipid nanoparticle library, potentially improving CNS penetration by 3x, and co-opting their AI-driven off-target prediction models, which boast 98% specificity. From a regional lens, this shores up our EU presence via Helix's ongoing interactions with EMA's PRIME scheme, while addressing U.S. CMC challenges through our existing Lonza manufacturing slots.

Finally, on partnerships, we expanded our existing alliance with AstraZeneca into a $500 million co-development pact for NOV-mRNA-789, our self-amplifying mRNA platform encoding IL-12/IL-15 fusion cytokines for checkpoint-refractory melanoma. Building on our 2022 discovery collaboration that yielded three hits, this deal includes $100 million upfront, $400 million in opt-in and development milestones, and 50/50 profit-sharing in the U.S./EU, with AZ handling ex-China commercialization. Early combo data with their Imfinzi showed a 48% mPFS extension versus monotherapy, tapping into the $25 billion IO combo market projected by 2028.

This partnership exemplifies our "portfolio-in-partnership" model, de-risking late-stage development while sharing costs—critical in an era of 15-20% YoY R&D inflation. Strategically, it diversifies our revenue beyond royalties into shared upside, mirroring Pfizer's Seagen playbook, and provides AZ optionality on two additional mRNA payloads in our immunology pipeline.

In aggregate, these BD activities have added $5.2 billion in total potential value to our pipeline NPV, with $395 million in near-term cash inflows bolstering our $2.8 billion pro forma cash position and extending runway to 2028. They've also diversified our modalities—now 40% small molecules/ADCs, 30% biologics, 20% gene editing, 10% mRNA—reducing binary risk and positioning us for the next wave of innovation amid headwinds like IRA pricing caps.

Looking ahead, we're advancing term sheets on two oncology in-licenses and scouting tuck-ins in radiopharma, where deals like Novartis' $2.1 billion Mariana Oncology acquisition signal frothy valuations but untapped potential. We're disciplined on multiples—targeting under 5x for pre-clinical and 3-4x for Phase 2 assets—and focused on platforms with multi-shot upside.

Thank you, Johnathan, and good afternoon, everyone. As we wrap up our Q3 earnings discussion, I'd like to dive deeper into one of the most critical areas for our long-term value creation: our patent cliff exposure and the proactive life cycle management—or LCM—strategies we're deploying across the portfolio. This is a classic Pharma challenge, but at BioNova Therapeutics, we've engineered a multi-layered defense that's not only mitigating downside risks but positioning us for sustained growth through the decade.

Let me start with the exposure. Our patent cliff profile is front-loaded but manageable, with approximately 38% of our projected 2025 revenue—roughly $4.2 billion out of $11.1 billion—at risk from primary patent expirations between 2027 and 2030. The biggest hitter is our blockbuster PD-1 inhibitor, OncoShield, which generated $3.8 billion in global sales last year, representing 42% of total revenue. Its core composition-of-matter patent expires in the U.S. in Q4 2027, with EU data exclusivity rolling off in mid-2028 and Japan following in 2029. Without intervention, we're modeling a steep erosion curve: 65-75% volume drop in Year 1 post-cliff in the U.S., accelerating to 85% by Year 3, based on historical analogs like Bristol Myers Squibb's Opdivo facing Keytruda dominance or AbbVie's Humira biosimilar onslaught starting in 2023, which saw U.S. sales plummet 35% in the first full post-cliff year despite HUMIRA's $14 billion-plus peak.

Compounding this, our legacy GLP-1 agonist for NASH, HepaRev, contributes another $1.1 billion annually and faces ANDA Paragraph IV challenges already in the queue, with first generic entry likely in 2029—earlier than our initial 2031 forecast due to aggressive Indian and Israeli filers. Regionally, the U.S. represents 55% of OncoShield's sales, where payer formulary pressures from the IRA's inflation rebate caps will amplify erosion. In Europe, EMA biosimilar approvals are moving faster; we've seen three adalimumab biosimilars launch since 2023, eroding originators by 90% within 18 months. China is our wildcard—HepaRev's local patent holds until 2032, but domestic biosimilars like those from Innovent are gaining traction via the NRDL, potentially capping our growth there at mid-single digits.

That said, we're not sitting idle. Our LCM playbook is battle-tested, drawing from successes like Merck's Keytruda label expansions that have extended its runway past $25 billion in annual sales despite 2028 patent expiry looming. We've invested $1.2 billion over the last three years in LCM, yielding a 2.5x ROI to date through extended exclusivities and new revenue streams. Let me break it down by pillar.

First, formulation and delivery innovations. For OncoShield, we've launched OncoShield SQ—a subcutaneous formulation approved via the 505(b)(2) pathway in the U.S. last quarter. This shifts from IV to self-admin at home, capturing 15-20% market share uplift in convenience-driven segments like adjuvant melanoma. Priced at a 10% premium, it's already ramping to $450 million in 2024 run-rate sales, with U.S. patent protection through 2036 and pediatric exclusivity adding six months. Globally, SQ filings are in late-stage review in EU and Japan, buffering the cliff by $1.8 billion in preserved peak sales.

Second, label expansions and combination therapies. Oncology is ripe for this—our Phase III data for OncoShield plus our in-house CDK4/6 inhibitor, NovaCycle, in HR+/HER2- breast cancer hit 72% PFS versus 55% for standard-of-care, triggering a BLA submission this fall. If approved by mid-2026, this combo could add $2.2 billion in incremental revenue by 2030, with method-of-use patents extending to 2039. We've also secured orphan drug designation for OncoShield in rare sarcomas, granting seven years U.S. exclusivity on top of our base IP. In NASH, HepaRev's fixed-dose combo with a novel FXR agonist—filed under 505(b)(1)—targets MASH patients, with topline data showing 45% fibrosis regression. This de-risks a $900 million cliff hit, with launch targeted for 2027 ahead of generics.

Third, evergreening and defensive IP strategies. We're leveraging every lever: supplemental NDAs for new polymorphs and enantiomers on HepaRev, pushing secondary patents to 2034; and litigating 17 Paragraph IV notices on OncoShield, settling five favorably to delay entries by 30 months on average. Our biosimilar defense fund stands at $800 million, modeled on Amgen's Enbrel playbook. In emerging markets, we're pursuing patent thickets—11 layered patents in China for OncoShield manufacturing processes—to slow local copycats.

Regional nuance is key. In the U.S., we're ahead of the curve with CMS negotiations; OncoShield's selected for 2027 price talks, but our LCM variants carve out exemptions under the IRA's biosimilar exclusion rules. Europe demands agility— we've preempted EMA cliffs with hybrid applications for OncoShield's bispecific evolution, maintaining 80% pricing power post-2028. In Asia-Pacific, Japan’s PMDA granted SAKIGAKE designation for our next-gen ADC, accelerating review and adding 10-year re-examination exclusivity.

Financially, these strategies transform our trajectory. Absent LCM, we'd see EBITDA margins compress 1,200 bps to 28% by 2030 from patent losses. With our plan, we limit it to 450 bps, holding at 52%, while growing patent-protected revenue share from 72% today to 68% in 2030—offset by $6.5 billion from pipeline launches like our bispecific T-cell engager in 2026. Free cash flow dips just 8% in 2028 versus a 25% modeled cliff, funding $15 billion in R&D through the decade.

Looking ahead, our LCM success rate is 85% on 12 initiatives since 2020, outpacing industry averages from McKinsey's 65%. We're on track for 8-10% CAGR through 2030, with ROIC above 15% on LCM assets. Risks remain—biosimilar pricing aggression, like the 40% discounts on Stelara in Europe—but our diversification into gene therapies (three in clinic with 2040+ IP) and ADCs positions us resiliently.

We're committed to maximizing shareholder value through smart IP stewardship.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Dr. Lisa Ramirez, our Chief Medical Officer, to discuss our clinical programs.

Dr. Lisa Ramirez, Chief Medical Officer:
Thank you, Michael. We are very pleased with the progress of our clinical trials. Specifically, thank you, Michael, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our clinical pipeline, which remains the cornerstone of BioNova Therapeutics' value creation strategy. As a clinical-stage biotech focused on next-generation antibody-drug conjugates, or ADCs, and bispecific T-cell engagers for solid tumors and hematologic malignancies, we're making strong progress across our portfolio. We've dosed over 1,200 patients cumulatively this year, with a 95% on-time milestone achievement rate—well above the industry average of 75% as reported in the BIO Clinical Development Success Rates study. Let me break this down by key programs, highlighting phase progressions, recent data readouts, and upcoming regulatory milestones.

Starting with our lead asset, BNV-301, our next-gen ADC targeting HER2-low breast cancer. We're thrilled with the Phase 2 topline readout from the HER2-LOW-202 study, announced last quarter. In 285 patients across 45 sites in the US and EU, we hit our primary endpoint of objective response rate, or ORR, with 52% in the 5.2 mg/kg cohort versus 28% for physician's choice chemo—statistically significant at p<0.001. Median progression-free survival, or PFS, was 9.4 months versus 5.2 months, a 44% improvement mirroring the success of Enhertu from Daiichi Sankyo/AstraZeneca. Notably, duration of response exceeded 12 months in 68% of responders, with a manageable safety profile: grade 3+ neutropenia at 22%, lower than the 35% seen in competitor profiles like Trodelvy. This positions BNV-301 as a potential best-in-class in the $4.5 billion HER2-low market, growing at 25% CAGR per Evaluate Pharma.

Enrollment is now complete in the pivotal Phase 3 BNV-301-301 trial, with 825 patients randomized 2:1 across North America, Europe, and China—where we've activated 15 sites through our partnership with Fosun Pharma to tap into the region's 20% annual breast cancer incidence growth. Topline PFS data expected Q4 2025, with overall survival interim in H1 2026. Regulatory-wise, we've secured FDA Fast Track and EMA PRIME designations, and plan BLA and MAA submissions in H2 2026, pending data. This de-risks our timeline and supports peak sales projections of $1.2 billion by 2032.

Moving to BNV-402, our bispecific T-cell engager for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma targeting BCMA and CD3. Phase 1b/2 data from the MYELOMA-BIS study, readout last month, showed a 78% ORR in 92 heavily pretreated patients—median 6 prior lines—outperforming Janssen's Tecvayli at 63% in similar populations. Complete response rates hit 42%, with cytokine release syndrome limited to grade 1/2 in 85% of cases via our proprietary step-up dosing. PFS not reached at 14 months median follow-up. Critically, in patients refractory to prior BCMA therapies like Carvykti, we saw 65% responses, addressing a key unmet need in the $15 billion myeloma space.

We've initiated the Phase 3 BNV-402-303 registrational trial, enrolling 650 patients globally, including expanded APAC sites in Japan under our PMDA consultation. Full enrollment by YE 2025, with data mid-2026. Orphan Drug and Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designations from FDA bolster our path to approval, and we're in talks for a co-development deal similar to Regeneron's Libtayo alliances, which could extend our $450 million cash runway into 2028.

In our earlier-stage pipeline, BNV-512, a KRAS G12C inhibitor ADC for non-small cell lung cancer, advanced from Phase 1 to Phase 2 initiation this quarter. Interim Phase 1 data in 36 patients showed 48% disease control rate at the RP2D, with intracranial responses in 3/5 brain mets patients—critical for the 30% of NSCLC with CNS involvement. We're aligning with the KRAS inhibitor surge post-Amgen's Lumakras, targeting a $3 billion addressable market.

Regionally, US trials represent 60% of our activity, with EU at 25% leveraging our MHRA alignment for UK approvals. China's contribution is ramping to 15% via Fosun, mitigating tariff risks amid US-China biotech tensions. Strategically, these updates validate our ADC platform's 85% Phase 1 to Phase 2 transition rate versus industry 70%, driven by our tumor-microenvironment selective linker tech. We've derisked four programs into Phase 3, positioning us for 2-3 approvals by 2027.

Looking ahead, key catalysts include BNV-301 Phase 3 enrollment completion Q3 2025, BNV-402 first Phase 3 data H1 2026, and an IND filing for BNV-512 combo with Keytruda in Q4. We're on track for a transformative readout season. We expect to achieve several upcoming milestones in these areas.

Next, Dr. Raj Patel will provide an update on our research pipeline.

Dr. Raj Patel, Chief Scientific Officer:
Thank you, Dr. Ramirez. We are making significant strides in our early-stage research. Our discovery engine continues to deliver novel candidates in gene editing and RNA therapeutics, with two new IND-enabling programs nominated this quarter in radiopharma and next-gen mRNA platforms. We've optimized our CRISPR/Cas13 libraries for neuromuscular targets, achieving 75% editing efficiency in non-human primates, and advanced AI models predicting off-target effects with 98% accuracy. These efforts complement our clinical portfolio and position us for multiple Phase 1 starts in 2025.

Now I'll turn the call over to Dr. Elena Vasquez, Head of Commercial, to discuss product sales and marketing.

Dr. Elena Vasquez, Head of Commercial:
Thank you, Dr. Patel. Our sales performance this quarter was outstanding, reflecting disciplined execution across regions. Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. This is Dr. Elena Vasquez, our Head of Commercial, stepping in to provide a deep dive into our marketing and sales effectiveness metrics for Q3.
